cards.Text: Where in the cell does HMP shunt activity occur? {{c1::Cytoplasm}}
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The HMP shunt may be referred to as the {{c1::pentose phosphate}} pathway
cards.Extra: AKA the 6-phosphogluconate pathway. Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: Does the HMP shunt use or produce ATP? {{c1::Neither}}
cards.Extra: No ATP is used or produced in the HMP shunt. Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The two products of the HMP shunt are {{c1::NADPH}} and {{c2::ribose-5-phosphate}}
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The rate-limiting enzyme of the HMP shunt is {{c1::glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase}} (G6PD)
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The oxidative phase of the HMP shunt is {{c1::irreversible}}; the non-oxidative phase is reversible
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: NADPH is produced only in the {{c1::oxidative}} phase of the HMP shunt
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: G6PD oxidizes glucose-6-phosphate and reduces NADP+ to {{c1::NADPH}}
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: Per glucose-6-phosphate, the oxidative phase yields {{c1::2}} NADPH, 1 CO2, and one pentose
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The CO2 of the HMP shunt is released by {{c1::6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase}}
cards.Extra: Also makes the 2nd NADPH. Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: Glucose-6-phosphate is ultimately converted to {{c1::ribulose}}-5-phosphate in the oxidative phase
cards.Extra: Then isomerized to ribose-5-phosphate. Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: Ribose-5-phosphate is the backbone for {{c1::nucleotides}} (DNA, RNA)
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The two enzymes of the non-oxidative phase are {{c1::transketolase}} and {{c2::transaldolase}}
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: Transketolase transfers {{c1::2}}-carbon units; transaldolase transfers 3-carbon units
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: Transketolase requires the cofactor {{c1::thiamine}} (TPP)
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The non-oxidative phase links to glycolysis through {{c1::fructose-6-phosphate}} and {{c2::glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate}}
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: HMP shunt activity is highest in the {{c1::adrenal}} cortex, liver, lactating mammary gland, and adipose
cards.Extra: Sites of NADPH-heavy synthesis. Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The HMP shunt occurs entirely in the {{c1::cytoplasm}}, not the mitochondria
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: G6PD is allosterically activated by {{c1::NADP+}} and inhibited by NADPH
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The main regulator of HMP shunt flux is the {{c1::NADPH/NADP+}} ratio
cards.Extra: Product inhibition of G6PD. Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: NADPH is required for {{c1::fatty acid}} synthesis, cholesterol synthesis, and glutathione reduction
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: NADH powers {{c1::catabolism}} (ATP); NADPH powers anabolism and antioxidant defense
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The structural difference between NADPH and NADH is an extra {{c1::phosphate}} group
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: In the red blood cell, the only source of NADPH is the {{c1::HMP shunt}}
cards.Extra: RBCs lack mitochondria. Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The first ROS formed when O2 gains one electron is {{c1::superoxide}}
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: Superoxide is converted to hydrogen peroxide by {{c1::superoxide dismutase}}
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: Hydrogen peroxide is neutralized by {{c1::catalase}} and glutathione peroxidase
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The most reactive ROS is the {{c1::hydroxyl radical}}
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The Fenton reaction generates the hydroxyl radical from H2O2 and {{c1::Fe2+}}
cards.Extra: Why free iron is dangerous. Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: Glutathione is a tripeptide of glutamate, {{c1::cysteine}}, and glycine
cards.Extra: The cysteine thiol does the work. Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The reduced, active form of glutathione is {{c1::GSH}}; the oxidized form is GSSG
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: GSH neutralizes hydrogen peroxide via the enzyme {{c1::glutathione peroxidase}}
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: GSSG is regenerated to GSH by {{c1::glutathione reductase}}, using NADPH
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The antioxidant chain is G6PD, then {{c1::NADPH}}, then GSH, which neutralizes ROS
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: About {{c1::0.2}}% of processed O2 escapes as superoxide
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The HMP shunt is favored when {{c1::NADPH}} is being consumed (high ATP, fed state)
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: A cell needing only ribose runs just the {{c1::non-oxidative}} phase, sparing G6PD
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: The non-oxidative phase is {{c1::reversible}}, so it can make ribose without the oxidative phase
cards.Extra: Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: Ribose-5-phosphate differs from deoxyribose by a hydroxyl on carbon {{c1::2}}
cards.Extra: Reduced (via NADPH) to make DNA. Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

cards.Text: {{c1::Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase}} deficiency is the most common enzymopathy worldwide
cards.Extra: ~400 million people. Photo credit: Ed Uthman, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr

cards.Text: The inheritance pattern of G6PD deficiency is {{c1::X-linked recessive}}
cards.Extra: Affects males more. Photo credit: Ed Uthman, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr

cards.Text: G6PD deficiency causes hemolysis only under {{c1::oxidative stress}}
cards.Extra: At rest, enough NADPH is made. Photo credit: Ed Uthman, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr

cards.Text: Oxidative triggers of hemolysis in G6PD deficiency include primaquine, sulfa drugs, dapsone, infection, and {{c1::fava beans}}
cards.Extra: Photo credit: Ed Uthman, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr

cards.Text: Hemolysis after eating fava beans is called {{c1::favism}}
cards.Extra: Photo credit: Ed Uthman, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr

cards.Text: The blood smear in G6PD deficiency shows {{c1::Heinz bodies}} and bite cells
cards.Extra: Photo credit: Ed Uthman, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr

cards.Text: Heinz bodies are precipitates of oxidized, denatured {{c1::hemoglobin}}
cards.Extra: Photo credit: Ed Uthman, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr

cards.Text: Bite cells form when {{c1::splenic macrophages}} remove Heinz bodies from RBCs
cards.Extra: Photo credit: Ed Uthman, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr

cards.Text: G6PD deficiency confers partial resistance to {{c1::malaria}} (P. falciparum)
cards.Extra: Common in malaria-endemic regions. Photo credit: Ed Uthman, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr

cards.Text: The antimalarial {{c1::primaquine}} classically triggers hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
cards.Extra: Photo credit: Ed Uthman, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr

cards.Text: In G6PD deficiency, oxidized hemoglobin and unprotected membrane lead to {{c1::hemolysis}}
cards.Extra: Photo credit: Ed Uthman, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr

cards.Text: The hemolytic crisis in G6PD deficiency is acute and {{c1::self-limited}} after the trigger
cards.Extra: Older RBCs lyse first. Photo credit: Ed Uthman, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr
